notes: On a 1:24 shell, coverage comes from three light coats — one heavy pass floods the door shuts and drowns the panel lines.
Retarder keeps the film open, so give each coat 25–30 min before the next or solvent gets trapped under the gloss.
Acrylic gloss almost never leaves the needle glass-smooth at this scale. Plan on clear over the top, then compound.
This is interior tub, floorpan, rollcage and engine-bay territory. Two light coats is plenty; flats bury fine moulded detail fast.
Hold back a little further on a floorpan so the sheen stays even across the whole panel.
Retarder helps here more than anywhere — flats are what clog a 0.3 mm nozzle mid-panel.
Semi-gloss is the right sheen for a 1:24 dashboard, wiper arms and window surrounds — flat reads chalky at this scale.
Sits between gloss and flat: thin a touch more than a gloss, a touch less than a flat.
Wheels, calipers, engine block, suspension: lay metallic over gloss black and the flake reads as polished metal instead of grey.
Drop the pressure and move in closer. High pressure scatters flake and it looks coarse against a 1:24 wheel face.
Stir, never shake. Shaking whips air in and the 0.3 mm nozzle spits it straight onto the part.
Metallics are fragile — mask over them with tape you've de-tacked on your sleeve first.
Over decals: mist coat first, leave it overnight, then go wet. A wet first pass on fresh decals silvers or lifts them.
For a 1:24 body, three thin clear coats beats one thick one — thick clear pools along the rocker panels and around mirrors.
Leave acrylic clear a full week before compounding. It feels hard long before it is.
Mist the first coat onto bare styrene. Wet lacquer straight onto raw plastic crazes fine detail like door shuts and badge outlines.
Over Tamiya lacquer primer it's very forgiving — that's the usual route to a polished 1:24 body colour.
Ventilate properly and wear a respirator; this is not the same risk level as the acrylics.
Decant into an open jar and wait 15–20 min until it stops fizzing, or propellant spits through the nozzle.
Rattle-can paint is already thinned to spray, so it only needs a small top-up to flow through a 0.3 mm needle.
Decanting is the standard trick for a 1:24 body: you get TS depth with airbrush control around the A-pillars and mirrors.

coats_text: Light coats from inside the shell
notes: PS is made for flexible RC polycarbonate bodies and sprays on the inside of the shell.
It will craze the hard styrene of a 1:24 kit body. Wrong paint for this build unless you're doing an RC shell.
On a car build enamel usually earns its place as a panel-line wash or engine-bay detail rather than a sprayed colour.
Leave it a full day before masking — enamel skins over long before it's hard underneath.
Keep enamel and its thinner away from stressed clear parts; windscreens craze.
Two thin coats on a 1:24 shell. Primer fills scribed panel lines faster than you'd expect.
Stir it hard — the filler settles into a solid plug at the bottom of the jar.
White primer shows every dust nib and sanding scratch, which is the point. Fix them now, not under the colour.
Not sprayed alone. X-20A is the retarder-type acrylic thinner itself — use it as the paint's thinner, roughly 1:1 into a gloss or 1:1.25 into a flat.

X-21 Flat Base knocks the sheen off a gloss or clear. Useful for seat fabric and dashboard tops on a 1:24 interior. Start at 1 part flat base to 8–10 parts paint, then thin the mix as normal — past about 20% it goes chalky and fragile.
Stir flat base hard before use — it settles into a solid plug.
